stance_summary: The Fed has hiked. After six consecutive holds the committee raised rates 25bp on Sept 16 — unanimously, despite widespread expectation of at least one dissent. The July dissenters won the argument and the rest of the committee came with them. The dot plot now points to another hike before year-end, with no cuts penciled in until 2028.
policy_outlook: The easing cycle is formally over. With one hike delivered and 16 of 18 participants projecting another before year-end, the question turns to pace: October or December, and whether the committee stops at two. No cuts are penciled in until 2028, and ten participants see none through 2029. Warsh has now survived his first genuine test of independence — hiking against explicit presidential pressure, with midterms weeks away.
alert: THE FED HIKED. September 15–16 meeting — FOMC raised the target range 25bp to 3.75%–4.00% on a unanimous 12–0 vote, the first increase since July 2023 and a sharp reversal of the easing cycle that ended in December. The 130-word statement: "Inflation remains elevated… Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal." The dot plot shows 16 of 18 participants expecting at least one more hike this year. Next meeting Oct 27–28.

members.name: Kevin Warsh
members.title: Chair, Board of Governors
members.note: Delivered the hike and held the committee together doing it. Called it "a sober decision, a serious decision, a responsible decision," said the move "removed a dose of accommodation," and that inflation has been "too high, for too long." Defied Trump's public demands for lower rates. Still declines to submit a dot.
members.latest_source: Sep 16 press conference; Aug 28 Jackson Hole

members.name: Jerome Powell
members.title: Board of Governors — permanent voter (former Chair)
members.note: Voted for the hike. Has kept the low profile he promised — no public commentary through the Jackson Hole repricing or the September decision. His Board seat continues to block a White House-preferred appointment.

members.name: Michael Barr
members.title: Vice Chair for Supervision
members.note: Voted for the hike, consistent with his pre-meeting signalling that he was open to moving in either direction depending on the data. The August core CPI overshoot settled it. Continues to weight financial stability alongside the inflation mandate.
members.latest_source: Sep 16 unanimous hike vote; early-Sep remarks

members.name: Michelle Bowman
members.title: Vice Chair for Supervision (acting)
members.note: Voted for the hike, abandoning the easing preference she held through the first half of the year. The energy-driven inflation she expected to fade instead reaccelerated, with Brent above $105 into the meeting. No longer a dovish vote in practice.

members.name: Lisa Cook
members.title: Board of Governors
members.note: Voted for the hike. Had flagged in an Aug 5 speech that core PCE at 3.3% was too high while arguing disinflationary forces could still do the work without tightening — the August data removed that option. Supreme Court removal case still pending.
members.latest_source: Sep 16 unanimous hike vote; Aug 5 speech

members.name: Philip Jefferson
members.title: Vice Chair
members.note: Voted for the hike. The centrist bloc he anchors moved as one — no Board member broke ranks despite the range of views aired publicly through August.

members.name: Christopher Waller
members.title: Board of Governors
members.note: The dissent that never came. Speculation before the meeting centred on Waller as the most likely holdout, given his January cut-dissent and cautious wait-and-see framing through the summer. He voted for the hike, completing the committee's realignment from cuts to tightening in eight months.

members.name: Stephen Miran
members.title: Board of Governors (serving on an expired term)
members.note: Voted for the hike — a remarkable arc for the member who dissented for cuts at every meeting in the first half of 2026. Three consecutive votes with the majority now. Still serving on an expired term pending a successor.

members.name: John Williams
members.title: NY Fed President — FOMC Vice Chair
members.note: Voted for the hike after signalling openness to it in early September, saying there were no clear signs whether policy was sufficient to bring inflation back to target. As FOMC Vice Chair his shift was an early tell that the hike had the votes.
members.latest_source: Sep 16 unanimous hike vote; early-Sep interview

members.name: Beth Hammack
members.title: Cleveland Fed President
members.note: Got what she dissented for. After hawkish dissents in April and July, the committee delivered her preferred action in September and she voted with it. Has cautioned that a single quarter point "does not do much" — likely among the four participants projecting two more hikes this year.
members.latest_source: Sep 16 unanimous hike vote; Jul 29 + Apr 29 dissents

members.name: Neel Kashkari
members.title: Minneapolis Fed President
members.note: Vindicated across the full arc: his early-2026 warning that an energy price shock could unanchor expectations became the committee's operating thesis, and his July dissent became September policy. One of the most complete stance reversals on the committee over the past two years.
members.latest_source: Sep 16 unanimous hike vote; Jul 29 + Apr 29 dissents

members.name: Lorie Logan
members.title: Dallas Fed President
members.note: Her formulation became the chair's. Warsh used "too high, for too long" — Logan's long-standing line on inflation — at the September press conference. Dissented in April and July; voted with the unanimous majority in September.
members.latest_source: Sep 16 unanimous hike vote; Jul 29 + Apr 29 dissents

members.name: Anna Paulson
members.title: Chicago Fed President
members.note: Voted for the hike. The dovish tail she represented has closed: unemployment held at 4.1% and the SEP revised the year-end projection down from 4.3%, removing the labour-market deterioration that underpinned her caution.
